title: Paper 2: Mathematical Reasoning
target_note: Reasoning, not algebra: the marks are in knowing which way an implication runs and what a negation actually says. Several questions have options that are all true, where only the logical form separates them.

questions.stem_html:
Consider the statement, about integers n:

If n2 is even, then n is even.

Which of the following is its contrapositive?

options.A: If n is not even, then n2 is not even.
options.B: If n is odd, then n2 is odd.
options.C: If n2 is odd, then n is odd.
options.D: If n is even, then n2 is even.
options.E: n2 is even if and only if n is even.
options.F: If n2 is not even, then n is not even.

questions.solution_html:
The contrapositive of 'if P then Q' is 'if not Q then not P': both parts negated and swapped.

Here P is 'n2 is even' and Q is 'n is even'. So not Q is 'n is not even', and not P is 'n2 is not even'.

The contrapositive is if n is not even, then n² is not even.

Every option here is a true statement, which is the point: truth is no guide to logical form. F negates both parts without swapping them — that is the inverse, and it is the option that catches most people.

traps.B: True, and logically equivalent to the contrapositive, but stated with 'odd' rather than as the negation of the original's own parts.
traps.C: True, but this is the contrapositive of the converse.
traps.E: A biconditional. True here, but it asserts more than the original does.
traps.F: The inverse: both parts negated, but not swapped.
traps.D: The converse: P and Q swapped without negating either.

questions.stem_html:
Consider:

For every real x, there exists a real y such that y2 = x.

Which of the following is the negation of this statement?

options.A: For every real x, there is no real y with y2 = x.
options.B: There exists a real x such that for every real y, y2 ≠ x.
options.C: There exists a real x and a real y with y2 ≠ x.
options.D: For every real y, there exists a real x with y2 ≠ x.
options.E: There exists a real y such that for every real x, y2 ≠ x.
options.F: For every real x, there exists a real y with y2 ≠ x.

questions.solution_html:
Negating swaps every quantifier and negates the predicate: ∀ becomes ∃, ∃ becomes ∀, and = becomes ≠. The order of the quantifiers does not change.

∀x ∃y (y2 = x) negates to ∃x ∀y (y² ≠ x).

Worth noticing: the original is false — take x = −1 — so its negation is true, and x = −1 is the witness.

C is the most tempting: it negates the predicate and makes both quantifiers existential, which is a much weaker claim and is trivially true of almost any pair.

traps.A: Far too strong: it claims no x has a square root at all.
traps.C: Both quantifiers existential — true, but a much weaker statement than the negation.
traps.D: The quantifiers have been reordered as well as swapped.
traps.E: x and y have swapped roles.
traps.F: Neither quantifier has been changed; only the predicate was negated.

questions.stem_html: Which of the following conditions on a real number x is necessary but not sufficient for x2 > 9?
questions.solution_html:
x2 > 9 is exactly |x| > 3, so C is necessary and sufficient — which disqualifies it.

A and B are sufficient but not necessary: x = −4 satisfies x2 > 9 without satisfying either.

D and E are neither: x = −4 again fails both while x2 > 9 holds, so they are not necessary.

x² > 0 is implied by x2 > 9 and does not imply it — x = 1 satisfies it and not the original.

Four of the six are eliminated by the single witness x = −4. Finding one good counterexample early is worth more than testing each option in turn.

traps.A: Sufficient but not necessary — x = −4 is a counterexample to necessity.
traps.B: Same as A, and also excludes x = 3 where x² = 9 anyway.
traps.C: Necessary AND sufficient — it is equivalent to the original.
traps.D: Neither: x = −4 satisfies x² > 9 but not x > 0.
traps.F: Neither, for the same reason as D.

questions.stem_html:
A student notices that n2 + n + 41 is prime for n = 1, 2, 3, … and conjectures that it is prime for every positive integer n.

What is the smallest positive integer n for which the conjecture fails?
questions.solution_html:
The expression factorises the moment n is a multiple of 41 — but it fails earlier than that.

At n = 40: 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 412.

Every value from n = 1 to 39 really is prime, which is why the conjecture is tempting in the first place.

n = 41 also fails — 412 + 41 + 41 = 41 × 43 — and is the failure most people remember. The question asks for the smallest, and 40 comes first.

traps.F: It fails; no polynomial in n is prime for every n.

questions.stem_html: Which of these statements about integers n is false?

options.A: n3 − n is divisible by 12 for every integer n.
options.B: n3 − n is divisible by 3 for every integer n.
options.C: n3 − n is divisible by 6 for every integer n.
options.D: n3 − n is divisible by 2 for every integer n.
options.E: n2 + n is divisible by 2 for every integer n.
options.F: n2 + n + 1 is odd for every integer n.

questions.solution_html:
n3 − n = (n−1)n(n+1): three consecutive integers. One is a multiple of 2 and one a multiple of 3, so the product is always divisible by 6. A, B and C all hold.

D is false. Take n = 2: 8 − 2 = 6, which is not a multiple of 12.

E and F are the same fact twice: n2 + n = n(n+1) is a product of consecutive integers and so always even, which makes n2 + n + 1 always odd.

The tempting reasoning for D is that among three consecutive integers you get a 2, a 3 and sometimes a 4. 'Sometimes' is the word that breaks it — and n = 2 is the smallest witness, not n = 3.

traps.B: True: one of any three consecutive integers is a multiple of 3.
traps.C: True: it follows from A and B, since 2 and 3 are coprime.
traps.E: True: n(n+1) is a product of consecutive integers.
traps.F: True, and it is just E restated.
traps.D: True: one of any two consecutive integers is even.

questions.detail: A divisibility claim that is nearly true

questions.stem_html: How many pairs of positive integers (x, y) satisfy x2 − y2 = 60?
questions.solution_html:
(x−y)(x+y) = 60. The two factors have the same parity, since their sum 2x is even — and since 60 is even, both must be even.

Write x−y = 2a and x+y = 2b: then 4ab = 60, so ab = 15 with b > a > 0.

That gives (a, b) = (1, 15) or (3, 5), so (x, y) = (16, 14) or (8, 2) — 2 pairs.

Listing the factor pairs of 60 gives six, and four of them — (1, 60), (3, 20), (4, 15), (5, 12) — mix parities and produce no integer solution at all. Checking parity first is the whole saving.

traps.C: Four counts the ordered sign variants, but x and y were required positive.
traps.D: Six is the number of factor pairs of 60; four of them fail the parity test.
traps.E: Twelve counts every factorisation including negatives.
traps.F: The factorisations of 60 are finite in number.

questions.stem_html:
a and b are real numbers with a2 = b2.

Which of the following must be true?
questions.solution_html:
a2 = b2 gives a2 − b2 = 0, so (a−b)(a+b) = 0 and therefore a = b or a = −b.

Either way the magnitudes agree, so |a| = |b| always holds — and it is the only option that covers both cases.

A, B, E and F each assert one branch of the 'or' as though it were the whole thing. D fails outright at a = b = 0.

This is the step behind most false proofs that 1 = 2: cancelling a square root and keeping only the positive branch.

traps.A: Only one of the two branches — a = 3, b = −3 is a counterexample.
traps.B: The other branch — a = b = 3 is a counterexample.
traps.D: Fails at a = b = 0, where ab = 0.
traps.F: This is A restated, and fails for a = 3, b = −3.
traps.C: This is B restated, and fails for a = b = 3.

questions.detail: What a² = b² does give you

questions.stem_html: For how many positive integers n is 2n ≤ n2?
questions.solution_html:
Check the small cases, which is all this needs:

n = 1: 2 > 1. n = 2: 4 = 4 ✓. n = 3: 8 > 9? No, 8 < 9 ✓. n = 4: 16 = 16 ✓. n = 5: 32 > 25.

From n = 5 onward the exponential stays ahead for good, so the answer is 3 — namely n = 2, 3 and 4.

Both n = 2 and n = 4 give equality, and the ≤ includes them. With a strict < the answer would be 1.

traps.A: n = 3 gives 8 < 9, so there is at least one.
traps.B: Two misses one of the equality cases, n = 2 or n = 4.

questions.detail: Where an exponential overtakes a square

questions.stem_html:
The statement 'if x > y then x2 > y2' is false for real x and y.

Adding which one of the following conditions makes it true?
questions.solution_html:
The counterexamples all have the larger number smaller in magnitude: x = 1, y = −5 for instance.

y ≥ 0 rules them out. If x > y ≥ 0 then both are non-negative and squaring preserves the order.

A fails: x = 1, y = −5. C fails: x = −1, y = −5 gives xy = 5 > 0 but 1 < 25. E adds nothing, since x > y already implies it.

D is the one worth a second look: x + y > 0 with x > y does force x > 0, and in fact makes the statement true — but so does B, and the question asks for a condition that works, with B the cleanest. Check D yourself: x = 3, y = −2 gives 9 > 4 ✓.

traps.A: x = 1, y = −5 satisfies x > y and x > 0, but 1 < 25.
traps.C: x = −1, y = −5 gives xy = 5 > 0, x > y, and 1 < 25.
traps.E: x > y already implies x ≠ y, so this adds nothing.
traps.F: y < 0 makes matters worse, not better — x = 1, y = −5.
traps.B: This does in fact repair it, but B is the standard and simpler condition; see the note.

questions.stem_html:
For which values of the real number k does

x2 − kx + 9 = 0

have two distinct positive real roots?
questions.solution_html:
Three conditions, all needed at once. Distinct real roots: k2 − 36 > 0, so |k| > 6.

Product of roots = 9 > 0, so they share a sign. Sum of roots = k, so that sign is positive exactly when k > 0.

Together: k > 6.

E is the trap for anyone who checks the discriminant and stops. k = −7 gives two distinct roots that are both negative.

traps.A: k = 1 gives no real roots at all.
traps.D: k = 6 gives a repeated root, which is not two distinct roots.
traps.E: k = −7 satisfies this and gives two negative roots.
traps.C: This range gives no real roots at all.

questions.detail: Necessary and sufficient for two positive roots

questions.stem_html: How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 200 are such that n2 ends in the digit 6?
questions.solution_html:
The last digit of n2 depends only on the last digit of n. Squaring 0–9 gives last digits 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1.

So n2 ends in 6 exactly when n ends in 4 or 6 — two of every ten.

In 1 to 200 that is 210 × 200 = 40.

Listing squares is hopeless in the time. The whole question is the observation that only the last digit matters, which takes one line to establish.

traps.A: Twenty counts only the numbers ending in 4, or only those ending in 6.
traps.B: Twenty-four does not correspond to any consistent rule here.
traps.D: Forty-four over-counts, usually by including numbers ending in 0.
traps.E: Fifty would be one in four.
traps.F: Eighty is four digits out of ten — but only two digits square to something ending in 6.

questions.stem_html: Which integers cannot be written as x2 − y2 for some integers x and y?

options.A: The integers that are 2 more than a multiple of 4
options.F: Every integer can be written this way

questions.solution_html:
x2 − y2 = (x−y)(x+y), and the two factors always have the same parity — their sum is 2x.

Both odd gives an odd product. Both even gives a product divisible by 4. There is nothing in between.

So the unreachable integers are exactly the ones that are even but not divisible by 4 — 2 more than a multiple of 4. The smallest is 2 itself.

Every odd number is reachable: 2k+1 = (k+1)2 − k2. That makes A the option most likely to be picked by someone who has only tried a few small cases.

traps.D: Every odd prime works, being odd; only the prime 2 fails, and it fails as an even number not a prime.

questions.detail: Which integers are a difference of squares

questions.stem_html:
For real p and q, the cubic x3 + px + q has three distinct real roots.

Which of the following must be true?
questions.solution_html:
The cubic has turning points only when p < 0, and it crosses the axis three times exactly when the two turning values straddle it.

Writing that condition out gives the standard discriminant: 4p³ + 27q² < 0.

B is implied by E — if 4p3 < −27q2 ≤ 0 then p < 0 — so B is also true. But E is the condition that is both necessary and sufficient, and B alone is not enough: p = −1, q = 10 has one real root.

Check the constant: 4 and 27, not 1 and 1. Option D is the same inequality with the coefficients forgotten, and it is wrong — p = −3, q = 4 satisfies D but the cubic has one real root.

traps.A: p > 0 gives a strictly increasing cubic and exactly one real root.
traps.B: Necessary, but not sufficient — p = −1, q = 10 has one real root.
traps.C: q = 0 is not required; x³ − 3x − 1 has three real roots.
traps.D: The right shape with the wrong coefficients; p = −3, q = 4 satisfies it and fails.
traps.F: This is the condition for exactly one real root.

questions.detail: When a depressed cubic has three roots

questions.stem_html: For how many prime numbers p is p2 + 2 also prime?
questions.solution_html:
Work modulo 3. Any prime other than 3 is congruent to 1 or 2 mod 3, and in both cases p2 ≡ 1, so p2 + 2 ≡ 0 mod 3 — and being bigger than 3, it is composite.

That leaves only p = 3: 9 + 2 = 11, which is prime.

So the answer is 1.

p = 2 is the natural first try: 4 + 2 = 6, not prime. Trying primes one at a time will convince you the answer is small but never that it is exactly one — only the mod 3 argument does that.

traps.C: Two would need a second prime; every p ≠ 3 gives a multiple of 3.
traps.F: The mod 3 argument rules out every prime except 3.

questions.detail: Primes whose square plus two is prime

questions.stem_html: What is the smallest positive integer n for which n! + 1 is not prime?
questions.solution_html:
1! + 1 = 2, 2! + 1 = 3, 3! + 1 = 7 — all prime.

4! + 1 = 25 = 52, which is not.

The argument that n! + 1 has no prime factor below n is correct and is often misremembered as proving primality. It only proves that any factor is larger than n — and 5 is larger than 4.

questions.stem_html: How many subsets of {1, 2, 3, …, 8} have an even sum? (The empty set counts, and its sum is 0.)
questions.solution_html:
The set has 28 = 256 subsets. Pair each subset with the one obtained by adding 1 if it is absent and removing it if it is present.

That pairing swaps the parity of the sum every time, and pairs every subset with exactly one other. So exactly half have an even sum: 128.

The four odd elements (1, 3, 5, 7) must be chosen an even number of times, giving 23 × 24 = 128 the long way. Both routes work; the pairing takes ten seconds.

traps.A: 64 is 2⁶ — a quarter of the subsets.
traps.B: 70 is ⁸C₄, the number of four-element subsets.
traps.C: 120 undercounts; the answer is exactly half of 256.
traps.E: 136 overcounts, usually by adding the empty set to an already complete count.
traps.F: 256 is every subset, not just those with an even sum.

questions.stem_html:
The statement 'if a divides bc then a divides b or a divides c' is false for positive integers.

Which of the following is a counterexample?
questions.solution_html:
A counterexample needs a to divide bc while dividing neither b nor c.

C: 4 divides 2 × 6 = 12, but 4 divides neither 2 nor 6.

In every other option a divides b outright, so the 'or' is satisfied and no counterexample arises.

The statement is true whenever a is prime — that is Euclid's lemma — so A, B, D and F can be discarded at sight, leaving only C and E to check.

traps.A: 2 divides 12, and 2 divides 4. Not a counterexample.

questions.stem_html:
A student solves x2 = 5x by dividing both sides by x to get x = 5.

How many real solutions does the equation actually have?
questions.solution_html:
x2 − 5x = 0 factorises as x(x − 5) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 5: 2 solutions.

Dividing by x assumes x ≠ 0, and that assumption throws away the root x = 0 without comment.

Never divide by an expression that can vanish — factorise instead. The same error is what makes most 'proofs' that 1 = 2 work.

traps.B: One is the student's answer — the root x = 0 was divided away.
traps.D: A quadratic has at most two roots.
traps.E: 5 is a root, not the number of roots.
traps.F: x² = 5x is not an identity; x = 1 fails it.

questions.stem_html: Let n be an integer. Which of these statements has a false converse?

options.A: If n is even then n2 is even.
options.B: If n2 is odd then n is odd.
options.C: If n is divisible by 6 then n is divisible by 2 and by 3.
options.E: If n is odd then n2 is odd.

questions.solution_html:
Turn each one round and look for a counterexample.

A and E are each other's converse and both hold; F is the converse of E. C's converse — divisible by 2 and by 3 implies divisible by 6 — is true, because 2 and 3 are coprime. D's converse, n + 1 = 3 implies n = 2, is true by arithmetic.

B's converse says n > 2 implies n > 3, and n = 3 refutes it.

Five of the six converses are true, so scanning for one that looks doubtful gets you nowhere — each has to be turned round and tested.

traps.A: Converse: if n² is even then n is even — true.
traps.C: Converse is true: 2 and 3 are coprime, so both together force 6.
traps.D: Converse is true: n + 1 = 3 gives n = 2.
traps.E: Converse: if n² is odd then n is odd — true.
traps.B: Converse: if n is odd then n² is odd — true.

questions.detail: A converse that happens to be false

questions.stem_html:
Consider these three statements about integers:

I. n2 + n is even for every integer n.
II. There is an integer n with n2 + n + 1 even.
III. n3 − n is divisible by 6 for every integer n.

Which are true?
questions.solution_html:
I: n2 + n = n(n+1), a product of consecutive integers, so always even. True.

II: since n2 + n is always even, n2 + n + 1 is always odd. No such n exists. False.

III: n3 − n = (n−1)n(n+1), three consecutive integers, divisible by both 2 and 3. True.

So I and III only.

II is an existence claim, and existence claims feel easy to satisfy — you only need one n. Here I has already ruled every n out, which is why reading the three statements together is faster than testing them separately.

traps.C: II is false: n² + n + 1 is always odd.
traps.E: II is false, and I is true.

questions.detail: Which of I, II and III hold
